newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand gets new bank chief as IMF aid sought.
newsitem.headline: Thailand gets new bank chief as IMF aid sought.

text.p: Thailand named a new central bank governor on Tuesday after political pressure forced the abrupt resignation of Bank of Thailand veteran Rerngchai Marakanond.

Financial markets applauded the appointment of Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi to the top central bank job and focused on the prospect of greater intervention by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Thailand's troubled economy.
Chaiyawat, like Rerngchai, is another 24-year central bank veteran.
The IMF, enlisted by the Thai government after initial reluctance, was expected to override the central bank and call the shots in running the economy in coming months, analysts said.
They said Chaiyawat, 50, would have his job shaped mostly by monetary and fiscal disciplines imposed by the IMF in the aftermath of Thailand's de facto devaluation of the local baht currency.
On Monday Thailand confirmed that it was seeking IMF advice to put its economy back on even keel and could possibly seek a credit line from the world body.
That decision overshadowed any impact that would normally arise from a change of its central bank governor, analysts said.

"It makes no difference who will be Rerngchai's successor in terms of policy. I would say for the next six months, the new governor would not have much choice but to walk the IMF line. His job would be made easier," said Kitti Limsakul, economics lecturer at Chulalongkorn University.
Few analysts were surprised by Rerngchai's resignation.
They said he had previously hinted he may quit. He was also seen as being closely associated with ex-Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan in resisting a baht devaluation.
Amnuay quit in June partly over policy conflicts with other cabinet ministers. Thailand let the baht float on July 2 and the currency has subsequently lost nearly 20 percent of its value.
"His resignation is a product of changing circumstances," Kitti said.
But Rerngchai did not leave without giving the government a parting shot.

"Like any human being...who is discouraged by sarcastic remarks and in order to protect my integrity and that of the Bank of Thailand, I would like to show my spirit by resigning from the governorship," Rerngchai said in a statement.
"My job so far has been strongly criticised and I faced consistent political pressure for me to leave office," he said.
Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh declined to say much about Rerngchai's departure after the cabinet meeting in northern Chiang Rai town.

"I am moved. He is an example of a man who worked for the good of the country," he said. "The transfers and removals are to create unity within the country's economic framework. If anything happens, I will be solely responsible."

Rerngchai's stout defence of his position confirmed market views that he was pressured to leave so Chavalit's government could forge ahead with its own agenda and appointees to fix an economy stumbling through its worst slump in over a decade.
"It's a pity that Rerngchai had to go but the government needed to clear the decks so it can make a fresh start now that it has sought IMF assistance," said a foreign debt analyst.
Rerngchai was blamed for the baht's disastrous showing following the managed float.
He also faced criticism for his handling of the troubled financial sector, which has been hit by a liquidity crunch and overexposure to depressed property firms.

"The politicians were taking some unfair shots at the man (Rerngchai) but they also had reasonable criticisms of him, like he waited too long to float the baht and spent a lot of national reserves in defending it," said another analyst at a foreign brokerage firm.
An IMF austerity package that could be adopted by Thailand would include tough measures aimed at improving the current account and balance of payments.

Kitti of Chulalongkorn University said that with Rerngchai and Amnuay gone, the pressure on shoring up the battered economy would rest on Prime Minister Chavalit and his new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya.
"Chavalit could not keep passing the buck. If the economy failed to show signs of bottoming out soon, the prime minister would also have to take the heat, politically," he said.
The economist said Chavalit and politicians in his six-party coalition would need agree to additional serious budget cuts which would likely be recommended by the IMF.
